Raised fields built in the shallow lakes of the Valley of Mexico, which fed Tenochtitlan and the Aztec cities. Farmers piled mud and plants into long, narrow beds, fenced them with stakes and planted willows at the edges, whose roots held the soil.

Canals ran between the beds. Farmers moved by canoe, scooped rich mud from the canals onto the fields and watered the crops easily. Seedlings were raised in nurseries and planted out. With this care, a chinampa could give several harvests a year of maize, beans, squash, chillies and flowers.

The system was much older than the Aztecs, but it grew hugely around the southern lakes of Xochimilco and Chalco from about the 1200s. Under Aztec rule, dikes kept the salty water of Lake Texcoco away from the fresh-water fields.

The Spanish drained most of the lakes after 1521. Chinampas still survive at Xochimilco in Mexico City, where tourists ride boats along the canals.
